```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.4, fig.height = 5.3, dpi = 220, out.width = "100%")

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, RcppRoll)

# Load all the functions for this question from the code folder
list.files("code/", full.names = TRUE) %>% .[grepl("[.]R$", .)] %>% walk(~source(.))

Funds <- Q3_Funds(read_rds("data/Active_Managers.rds"), read_rds("data/ABC_Fund.rds"))
Bench <- Q3_Bench(read_rds("data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds"))
Cash  <- Q3_Cash(read_rds("data/STeFI_Index.rds"))

Roll_Beta <- Q3_Rolling_Beta(Funds, Bench, Window = 36)
PCA       <- Q3_PCA(Funds, Months = 60)
Rank      <- Q3_Rolling_Rank(Funds, Window = 36)
Score     <- Q3_Scorecard(Funds, Bench, Cash)
Disp      <- Q3_Market_Dispersion(read_rds("data/Monthly_Index_Constituents.rds"), read_rds("data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds"))
ABC_M     <- Q3_ABC_Monthly(Funds, Bench, Disp)
Alpha     <- Q3_Alpha(Funds, Bench, Cash)
PCA_F     <- Q3_PCA_Prac(Funds, Months = 60)

# On a slide the frame title carries the message, so the chart's own title is dropped
# and its subtitle (which explains what is plotted) is wrapped to fit the column.
Slide <- function(g, Wrap = 70) {
    if (!inherits(g, "ggplot")) return(g)
    g + labs(title = NULL, subtitle = str_wrap(g$labels$subtitle, Wrap))
}
```

# Beyond market beta

## Most active managers are largely market exposure

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r beta-box}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Beta_Box(Q3_Beta_Snapshots(Roll_Beta))) +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 2.2)))      # room for the "ABC Fund" label
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- **Beta** measures how far a fund moves with the market: a beta of 1 means it rises and falls one-for-one with the Capped SWIX.
- Since 2018 the typical peer's beta has been **0.8--0.9**, so much of what clients pay active fees for is market exposure.
- ABC sits below the peer range every year, and its beta has fallen to **about 0.4**.
:::
::::::

## The market explains less than half of ABC's returns

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r beta-r2}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Beta_R2(Roll_Beta))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- **R-squared** is the share of a fund's monthly returns that the market explains.
- For most peers it is **over 80%**; for ABC it is **about 40%**, lower than for 95% of peers.
- Most of ABC's return therefore comes from the manager's own positions, not from the market.
:::
::::::

## The industry moves as one herd; ABC does not

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r drivers}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Drivers(PCA))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- Principal component analysis on five years of peer returns finds the industry's common drivers directly.
- One driver, essentially the market, explains **87%** of the typical peer's returns.
- For ABC it explains **59%**, and 95% of peers are more tied to it: ABC adds a different return stream to a portfolio.
:::
::::::

## One common factor explains 82% of peer returns

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r pca, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
Plot_Q3_PCA_Prac(PCA_F, NComp = 6)
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- **Scree plot:** the first component explains **82%** of peer return variation; no other explains more than 3.5%.
- **Circle:** almost every peer arrow reaches the edge along component 1 (median correlation 0.93).
- **ABC**, added without influencing the components, has a shorter arrow (0.77) that points towards a second theme (0.30) most peers lack.
:::
::::::

# Track record

## A top-quartile fund 70% of the time since 2015

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r rank}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Rank(Rank))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- ABC's rank among peers on rolling 3-year returns (100th percentile = best fund).
- In the **bottom quartile only 2%** of the time, with its strongest run in 2020--2022.
- The **2025 dip** (to about the 22nd percentile) is real: a lower-beta fund lags a strong, broad rally, the flip side of its protection.
:::
::::::

## Ahead of about 90% of peers on every key measure

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r scorecard}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Scorecard(Score))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- **Return:** 11.9% a year against 8.2% for the median peer (2015--2025).
- **Risk:** lower volatility (11.1% vs 13.4%) and half the maximum drawdown (-13.7% vs -26.2%).
- **Risk-adjusted:** a Sharpe ratio of 0.48 against 0.18. More return with less risk is rare among active managers.
:::
::::::

# Protection and skill

## The dispersion claim does not hold up

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r dispersion}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Dispersion(ABC_M))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- **Dispersion** measures how far apart stock returns are in a month. The claim: ABC does best when it is high.
- ABC's excess return is, if anything, **slightly lower** in high-dispersion months; regression slopes are not significant (p = 0.71 and 0.99).
- Drop this claim with clients: the next slide has the message the data supports.
:::
::::::

## Where ABC earns its place: when markets fall

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r market-regimes}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Market_Regimes(ABC_M))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- In the market's worst quarter of months the Capped SWIX fell **4.6%** on average, the median peer **3.5%** and ABC only **1.7%**.
- ABC captures about **39%** of the market's falls against about 75% for the typical peer; only 1% of peers protect better.
- It gives up some upside in the best months (3.9% vs 6.0%), but losing less in bad months compounds into a better long-run return.
:::
::::::

## Skill or luck? ABC's alpha beats 98% of peers

:::::: {.columns align=center}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r alpha}
Slide(Plot_Q3_Alpha(Alpha))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
\small

- **Alpha** is the return earned beyond what market exposure explains.
- ABC: **3.6% a year**, higher than 98% of peers; the median peer's alpha is slightly negative (-0.3%).
- A t-statistic of 1.76 (p = 0.08) is just below the usual bar of 2, which only 3% of peers clear: strong evidence, not proof.
:::
::::::

## Why include ABC in client portfolios

:::::: {.columns align=top}
::: {.column width="50%"}
\small

**The case**

- **A genuine diversifier:** most of its return comes from the manager's own decisions, not from the market or the industry herd.
- **Downside protection:** it loses far less than peers and the market when markets fall.
- **Proven over time:** top-quartile 70% of the time, and an alpha of about 3.6% a year, among the highest in the peer group.
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
\small

**Points to note**

- ABC tends to lag in the strongest rallies, as in 2025.
- The dispersion argument is not supported and should not be used.
- Past performance does not guarantee future results.

\vspace{0.6em}
\scriptsize \color{abcgrey} Data notes: peer returns are winsorised each month at the 1st and 99th percentiles (one fund reports -55\% in its final month before closing). Benchmark-based measures use the Capped SWIX from January 2015. Funds that closed are included while they were active.
:::
::::::
